entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Zababa-šuma-iddina, the 35th and penultimate king of the Kassite (or 3rd) dynasty of Babylon, reigned for a solitary year around 1158 BCE, marking a pivotal moment in Mesopotamia's Late Bronze Age. His ascension to the throne remains shrouded in mystery, as he appears to have lacked direct ties to the established Kassite royal lineage, suggesting a period of significant internal instability within the Babylonian kingdom. This brief and tumultuous reign culminated in the catastrophic Elamite invasion, which not only ended his rule but irrevocably shattered the nearly four-century-long Kassite dominion over Babylonia, fundamentally reshaping the region's political landscape.

The core event of Zababa-šuma-iddina's short tenure was the devastating campaign launched by the Elamite king Shutruk-Nahhunte I. Capitalizing on Babylonian weakness, Shutruk-Nahhunte I led his forces into Mesopotamia, decisively defeating Zababa-šuma-iddina and sacking the venerable city of Babylon. This conquest was not merely a change of rulers; it involved the systematic plunder of Babylon's most sacred treasures and cultural artifacts, including the revered stele of Naram-Sin and the Law Code of Hammurabi, which were carried off to Susa as spoils of war. The profound humiliation and material losses inflicted during this period signaled the complete collapse of Kassite authority.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Zababa-šuma-iddina's reign, though brief, is historically significant as it marked the definitive end of the 400-year-old Kassite Dynasty and ushered in a period of Elamite dominance, profoundly altering the geopolitical landscape of Mesopotamia.
